preamble: Loss of glottalization in the glottalized lateral [lˀ] (Americanist l̓, written l' in the practical orthographies). In Upriver Halkomelem (Halq'eméylem) the glottalized resonants lost their glottalization, usually lengthening the preceding vowel, while Island and Downriver Halkomelem keep them (Compton & Gerdts c. 2005; Wikipedia says glottalized resonants are absent from most Upriver dialects). Island and Downriver qel'q 'wild rose' thus corresponds to Upriver qe:lq. For the Chimakuan languages, the correspondence table in Wikipedia's Chimakuan languages article (after Powell 1974) gives the reflexes of the glottalized resonants as R or ʔR, with *l̓ appearing as l or ʔl in both Quileute and Chemakum. The Quileute words in the same article's numeral table, such as ḳʷáʔl 'three', show a glottal stop followed by a plain resonant, so the glottalization may survive as a separate segment rather than be lost; they are not listed as examples here.

examples.note: Compton & Gerdts (c. 2005), plants page and 'Sounds of Halkomelem'; the shrub name is qel'qulhp vs Upriver qe:lqulhp. The site's consonant chart writes the glottalized resonants m' n' l' y' w', and its sounds page marks a long vowel with a following colon.
Wiktionary (stó:lō) lists stal̓əw̓ as the Hən̓q̓əmin̓əm̓ form of the same word. No Proto-Salish form of either example word was found online.
